How Binance Is Built to Absorb Extreme Events

2026-11-20

Main Takeaways

  • As of November 13, 2026, Binance has replaced 100% of the affected token assets from its own funds following the October 29, 2026 security incident. 

  • Our latest Proof of Reserves snapshot, taken at 00:00 UTC on November 12, 2026, shows 100% backing across 198 tokens.

  • In this post, we explain how our emergency funds cover losses and how Proof of Reserves lets you verify that user assets are backed 1:1.

On October 29, 2026, Binance experienced a security incident that affected around $6.3 billion in digital assets. Our initial incident report explains what happened and the steps we have taken since. 

As of November 13, 2026, 100% of the affected token assets have been replaced. If you hold any of the affected tokens, you can verify your assets are backed 1:1 through our Proof of Reserves (PoR) page.

Since the incident, many people inside and outside our community have asked how an exchange can absorb a loss that size without passing it on to users. Here’s how our emergency funds covered the loss, and how Proof of Reserves lets you check the backing yourself.

How Binance Covered the Loss

Binance, not our users, paid for the loss. 

We held more than 100% of the funds needed to cover it across three sources:

  • Part of the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU)

  • Part of our Futures insurance fund

  • Our corporate treasury

When our systems flagged the large transfers, we suspended withdrawals and worked with partners to freeze the affected tokens. As per our November 3 update, about $2.85 billion of the affected assets were frozen or intercepted. On November 18, 2026, Binance was granted a court order in the Abu Dhabi Global Markets (ADGM) Courts to support the recovery of assets connected to the incident. Issuers, exchanges, and other partners sometimes ask for a formal court order before they release, transfer, or return frozen assets, and this order helps create that pathway. Recovery will take time, and we will share updates as it progresses.

What is the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU)?

We established SAFU in July 2018 as an emergency reserve to protect user assets in extreme cases, such as security breaches or platform-level incidents. We built the fund over time by setting aside a percentage of trading fees until it reached approximately $1 billion. Since early 2026, SAFU has been held entirely in bitcoin.

We used part of SAFU to help cover the October 29 incident, alongside our corporate treasury and part of our Futures insurance fund. This is the kind of event the fund was built for. We are also committed to replenishing SAFU to approximately $1 billion.

The industry has seen many hacks and security incidents over the years, and in many of them, users lost funds. We built our emergency measures on the lessons from those cases. SAFU, our Futures insurance fund, and our corporate treasury are all kept separate from user assets. 

Most importantly, we put the safety of user assets above everything else.

Proof of Reserves Explained

In 2022, we introduced a Proof of Reserves (PoR) system to show that all user assets are backed 1:1. For every coin you hold on Binance, we hold at least one in reserve. You don’t have to take our word for it. You can check the PoR page at any time.

Think of an auditor who can confirm a bank's total deposits without reading anyone's account statement. PoR works in a similar way. Our first version used a Merkle tree, a method that combines every user's balance into a single code called a Merkle root. 

When community members raised concerns about privacy and possible manipulation, we added zk-SNARKs in February 2023. A zk-SNARK is a zero-knowledge proof that confirms something is true without revealing the underlying data. 

Our PoR shows full backing without exposing anyone's balance, and lets you confirm that your own balance is included in the total. It also includes user debt and collateral, so the figures reflect the true amount Binance owes users, including those who borrow. 

Moreover, we have expanded PoR coverage to 198 tokens. The latest snapshot, taken on November 12, 2026, shows that BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC, among others, are all 100% (or more) backed.

Final Thoughts

As of November 13, 2026, we have replaced 100% of the affected token assets. Proof of Reserves is always available, so you can check reserves on the PoR page at any time.

Since the incident, we have rebuilt the affected wallet system, tightened our controls, and continued to expand our investment in AI-powered security. For all updates, please refer to our official channels, including X, Announcements, and the Blog.

  • Binance Security Incident

Yield-Bearing Collateral: How VIP and Institutional Users Put Assets to Work on Binance

2026-11-19

Main Takeaways

  • RWUSD, BFUSD, and LDUSDT are three yield-bearing assets on Binance that keep earning while they serve as collateral.

  • This guide explains each asset’s use cases. RWUSD and BFUSD both back Futures, Margin, and VIP Loan positions, while LDUSDT turns Simple Earn USDT into USDⓈ-M margin.

  • Review redemption terms before you commit: redemption routes, timing, and limits differ by asset and matter more as positions grow.

Some balances have one job: be there when needed. Reserves set aside to back a loan, or margin a futures desk posts so its positions can run. To do that job, the balance stays locked. But locked balances earn nothing. The more you hold as collateral, the more you leave idle.

It doesn’t have to work that way. RWUSD, BFUSD, and LDUSDT are yield-bearing assets on Binance that keep earning rewards while they serve as collateral, so a balance can do its job and earn at the same time. 

This guide shows how each one works as collateral, which balance it suits, and what to check on redemption before you commit, including at larger sizes. It’s built to be kept, so come back to it whenever you need it, and share it with your team.

Three Assets Cover Three Different Collateral Jobs

Collateral rarely sits in just one place, so no single asset fits every balance. RWUSD, BFUSD, and LDUSDT each suit a different kind of balance. Each profile below covers what it is, how it works, and how it serves as collateral, so you can find your fit.

RWUSD: Treasury-Benchmarked Rewards on Your Stablecoin Reserves

If you hold stablecoin reserves and want rewards at a relatively stable APR, RWUSD earns daily, benchmarked against U.S. Treasury yields, while serving as margin for Futures Trading or as collateral for VIP Loans and Margin Trading.

  • What it is, and isn’t: RWUSD is an Earn product with flexible-term subscriptions and daily rewards. Rewards are supported by strategies including tokenized U.S. Treasuries managed by BlackRock, Circle, and Franklin Templeton, and income from Binance’s ecosystem. It is not a stablecoin or security, and gives you no ownership of anything underlying.

  • How it works: You subscribe with an eligible stablecoin and receive RWUSD 1:1 in your Spot Account, with no subscription fee. Rewards start accruing the day after your subscription and are distributed daily in RWUSD to your Spot Account. Redeem RWUSD back to USDC at 1:1 through Fast Redemption or Standard Redemption.

  • Collateral use: You can use RWUSD as margin for Futures Trading, or as collateral for VIP Loans and Margin Trading, while it continues to earn rewards.

BFUSD: Funding-Rate Rewards on Your Futures, Margin, and VIP Loan Collateral

If you hold balances as Futures, Margin, or VIP Loan collateral and are comfortable with rewards that move with funding rates, convert USDT to BFUSD and it keeps earning rewards while it supports your positions. You can redeem it for USDT when you need to, subject to redemption limits and fees, so review them before you size a position around BFUSD.

  • What it is, and isn’t: BFUSD is a reward-bearing margin asset that you can redeem for USDT. It earns daily rewards on qualifying balances. It is not a stablecoin.

  • How it works: BFUSD converts to and from USDT at 1:1, with no subscription fee, though redemption fees may apply. Its rewards come mainly from funding fees on delta-neutral hedges, plus staking rewards.

  • Collateral use: You can hold BFUSD as margin in Futures (Multi-Assets Mode and Portfolio Margin) and Margin accounts, or use it as collateral for VIP Loans.

LDUSDT: Put Simple Earn USDT to Work as USDⓈ-M Margin

If you hold USDT in Simple Earn and also trade USDⓈ-M Futures, LDUSDT lets the same balance do both jobs. It keeps earning its Simple Earn Real-Time APR while it serves as your margin, so you don't have to choose between earning and trading.

  • What it is, and isn’t: LDUSDT is a reward-bearing margin asset for USDⓈ-M Futures. It is not a stablecoin.

  • How it works: You swap USDT held in Simple Earn for LDUSDT, and the LDUSDT is moved to your Futures Account. You keep earning the Simple Earn APR while you use it as margin.

  • Collateral use: LDUSDT works as margin on the USDⓈ-M Futures platform in Multi-Assets Mode. Your Simple Earn Flexible USDT position can also be pledged directly as collateral for Flexible Rate Loans and VIP Loans, with no swap needed.

Choosing Between RWUSD, BFUSD, and LDUSDT as Collateral

RWUSD suits stablecoin reserves where steady, predictable rewards matter most. BFUSD suits Futures, Margin, or VIP Loan collateral where you’re comfortable with rewards that move with funding rates, which can be relatively higher when rates are positive. LDUSDT suits Simple Earn USDT that also serves as USDⓈ-M margin.

The comparison below sets out what each one is, where its yield comes from, how you get it, and which balance it suits. Please note that redemption works differently for each asset.

How VIP Desks Use RWUSD, BFUSD, and LDUSDT: An Illustrative Scenario

Collateral looks tidy on a balance sheet but can get complicated at the desk. 

Picture a VIP desk with one pool of stablecoin and two jobs for it: reserves that should earn at a steady rate, and collateral that can take on more variable rewards.

Here’s one way to split it. Reserves the team wants earning at a steady rate go into RWUSD. It earns daily rewards at a relatively stable APR, and can serve as Futures margin, Margin Trading collateral or, where the team is eligible, collateral for a Binance VIP Loan. 

Collateral where the desk can take on more variable rewards goes into BFUSD, which can back the same positions and earns from funding fees, so its yield can be relatively higher when funding rates are positive.

A desk that already holds Simple Earn USDT and trades USDⓈ-M Futures in Multi-Assets Mode has a third route: swap into LDUSDT instead, and the same balance keeps earning the Simple Earn APR while it serves as margin. 

In each case, the balance does its job and keeps earning.

Redeeming RWUSD, BFUSD, and LDUSDT

Redemption terms matter more as a position grows, so review each asset’s options before you size a position around it.

RWUSD can be redeemed to USDC at a 1:1 ratio through two routes: Fast Redemption and Standard Redemption. Fast Redemption returns USDC instantly, charges a 0.1% fee, and is subject to a daily redemption quota. Standard Redemption returns USDC on the T+3 day, charges a 0.05% fee, and is subject to a daily quota of 1.5 million USDC. For full details, see the RWUSD FAQ.

BFUSD also offers two routes. Fast Redemption is real-time and costs 0.1%, with a daily limit of 10,000 BFUSD for standard holders and 500,000 BFUSD for large holders. Standard Redemption costs 0.025%, takes 2 days, and has a daily limit of 10,000,000 BFUSD. In extreme market conditions, redemption can be delayed for up to 7 days, and Binance may adjust redemption fees at its discretion. For full details, see the BFUSD FAQ.

LDUSDT returns to Simple Earn USDT through a swap back, which can be done at any time, with the USDT deposited directly into your Earn Account. The conversion rate is at least equal to your original rate, so the swap back won’t reduce your balance. For full details, see the LDUSDT FAQ.

Redeeming at Scale and Speed with OTC & Execution Services

Each route above is designed around daily quotas and settlement windows. Both Fast and Standard Redemption are subject to daily limits, and Standard Redemption settles within two to three days, depending on the asset. For positions larger than a single day’s quota, a redemption may take longer and be spread across several days.

For redemptions of US$200,000 equivalent or more, Binance OTC & Execution Services offers an additional route. Our traders support each redemption directly, with settlement typically within 20 minutes.

Clients can reach the service directly from the Binance OTC trading portal.

Final Thoughts

Collateral has to stay in place, and the more you hold, the more sits idle.

RWUSD, BFUSD, and LDUSDT let that balance earn while it stays in place. Which one fits comes down to where the balance sits: stablecoin reserves; Futures, Margin, or VIP Loan collateral; or Simple Earn USDT.

The other half of the decision is redemption. Redemption routes, timing, and limits differ by asset, and they matter more as a position grows, so check them before you commit. For larger positions, Binance OTC & Execution Services is one option. The decision stays with you.

Keep this guide close, so the next time a balance needs a job, you already know where to start.

  • Binance VIP Earn

  • Binance VIP Program

DISCLAIMER: The value of your investment may go down or up and you may not get back the amount invested. APR refers to cryptocurrency rewards, not actual or predicted returns in fiat currency. RWUSD is not directly linked to real assets or securities and is not available to U.S. persons. Reward APR is discretionary and may change. RWUSD involves risks and redemption is not guaranteed to be immediate. BFUSD cannot be withdrawn, and redemption restrictions may apply, which may affect your ability to redeem BFUSD for a supported USD stablecoin. Not financial advice. For more information, see our Terms of Use and Risk Warning.

Global Policy Insights: CeFi to DeFi

2026-11-19

Prepared by 

  • Steven McWhirter, Global Policy Lead

  • Diego Montes Serralde, Global Policy Manager

Binance Global Policy Insights | November 2026

Main Takeaways

  • CeFi and DeFi are increasingly finding synergies, with clearer pathways that let users choose when to use each model. A CeDeFi approach is emerging which combines CeFi’s accessible interfaces, access, scale, and operational safeguards with DeFi’s on-chain transparency and permissionless innovation, while seeking to maintain a clear boundary between custodial services and self-custody experiences. 

  • Binance’s Hybrid Ecosystem: Binance provides examples of CeFi–DeFi synergies through an ecosystem that brings together a leading CeFi platform with access to public blockchain infrastructure. Binance’s centralised exchange offers liquidity, security features, and user-friendly access, while BNB Chain is a public, decentralised blockchain ecosystem that supports on-chain applications and innovation. Users can connect between account-based services and on-chain activity through bridging infrastructure and wallet integrations, including Binance Wallet, which can help users move assets across supported networks with reduced friction.

  • Bridging Products and Services: Binance’s major products illustrate CeDeFi interplay. Binance Launchpad helps new blockchain projects reach millions of users through the exchange, then flourish on decentralised networks. Binance Launchpool lets users lock assets on the CeFi platform to receive token rewards, connecting centralised participation with projects that may subsequently develop broader on-chain utility. Institutional custody and settlement arrangements can also provide more controlled pathways through which eligible institutions access exchange-linked liquidity and, where appropriate, on-chain opportunities. Binance Wallet integration is an easily accessible self-custodian tool, allowing users to access dApps and other DeFi features.

  • A Potential Blueprint for Finance: CeDeFi’s hybrid approach may serve as a blueprint for the broader industry. CeDeFi suggests that access to decentralised yield opportunities can be structured alongside compliance frameworks, and that institutional trust and open innovation can reinforce each other rather than conflict. Institutions can access on-chain opportunities through more structured risk management pathways, while retail users retain greater choice over how and where they interact with decentralised applications.

1 / Introduction

For years, the crypto industry framed CeFi and DeFi as competing models. CeFi emphasized convenience, liquidity, and familiar account-based experiences, while DeFi prioritized transparency, programmability, independence and user-controlled assets.

In practice, most users want elements of both. They want straightforward onboarding, deep markets, and strong operational standards, while also having the option to access permissionless applications on public blockchains. This article looks at how that convergence is unfolding, using Binance’s ecosystem as a practical example of how CeFi and DeFi can connect in one user journey and what it implies for the allocation of custody, execution, and risk across services.

2 / What Do We Mean by CeFi and DeFi?

CeFi and DeFi describe where custody, execution, and control sit in a financial experience. One model is not inherently “better” for every use case, and the most effective systems increasingly combine them.

In regulatory discussions, the distinction between CeFi and DeFi increasingly turns not only on the decentralised nature of the underlying technology, but also on the governance and functions surrounding it. The FATF’s 2026 analysis, for example, distinguishes the underlying smart-contract technology from the broader DeFi arrangement and focuses on whether identifiable persons exercise control or sufficient influence over how financial services are provided.

CeFi and DeFi from competition to convergence

The industry is moving beyond a binary “CeFi versus DeFi” debate. The more strategic question is how to combine strengths in a way that improves outcomes for users and supports institutional participation.

Where there is clear functional and legal segregation between the underlying infrastructure and persons providing financial services around it, regulatory treatment can reflect the actual allocation of control, influence and risk. Hybrid models may raise more complex questions where centralised entities facilitate access to DeFi arrangements, particularly where they exercise control or sufficient influence over the services provided or actively facilitate activities that fall within the scope of financial regulation.

This blended approach is often described as CeDeFi. In practice, CeDeFi is often described as a design pattern: it connects CeFi’s usability and liquidity with DeFi’s open infrastructure and programmable markets. It aims to make on-chain participation more accessible without stripping users of the option to self-custody and interact directly with protocols.

The enabling layer for this convergence is infrastructure. When networks are scalable and wallets and bridges are secure and easy to use, moving between custodial services and on-chain applications becomes a normal product flow.

3 / Binance’s Hybrid Crypto Ecosystem

Binance brings together centralised financial services and technical interfaces that facilitate access to independent public blockchain ecosystems, including BNB Chain. Through its exchange, wallet integrations and supported cross-chain connectivity, Binance helps users move between custodial services and on-chain applications while preserving the distinct governance, control and risk characteristics of each environment.

A. CeFi pillar: Binance’s centralised services 

The foundation of Binance’s ecosystem is the Binance Exchange. This is a centralised cryptocurrency exchange at massive scale, serving over 300 million users globally, where users can trade hundreds of cryptocurrencies in a custodial setting. The Binance Exchange provides centralised market access, liquidity, and an account-based experience that many users rely on for trading and portfolio management.

At its core, the Binance Exchange provides high-performance spot, margin, and derivatives venues, integrated with reliable fiat on- and off-ramps so newcomers can buy their first asset in a familiar environment while advanced users execute complex strategies at scale.

This layer is underpinned by a trust architecture built for operational assurance. Assets are safeguarded through robust custody controls, a public proof-of-reserves program intended to provide transparency regarding asset backing, and the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) as an additional contingency. Together, these controls provide transparency, loss-absorption capacity, and day-to-day resilience.

For institutions, independent custody and settlement providers can offer additional pathways to access exchange liquidity. Ceffu provides institutional custody solutions, while its MirrorX offering enables eligible institutions to access Binance Exchange liquidity through off-exchange settlement arrangements, with assets remaining in Ceffu's custody subject to the applicable operational and legal framework.

On the portfolio side, Simple Earn offers flexible and locked options for earning rewards by depositing digital assets, Auto-Invest supports recurring accumulation, and Binance Loans, including VIP facilities, supports over-collateralized liquidity without forcing users to unwind core positions. These tools let users manage returns, build positions methodically, and unlock funding from a single account.

Beyond trading and earning, CeFi can support real-world utility. Binance Pay is positioned as a crypto payments technology for sending and receiving crypto and paying merchants in supported contexts.

B. DeFi pillar: BNB Chain and decentralised platforms

On the decentralised side, BNB Chain provides public blockchain infrastructure for smart contracts and applications. It is a public, open-source smart contract ecosystem supported by a distributed ecosystem of validators, developers, and contributors, designed to host a wide range of decentralised applications (dApps). BNB is used as the network’s gas token for transactions and as the staking asset within its validator-based consensus model. BNB Chain operates independently of Binance Exchange. Its underlying infrastructure is maintained through its decentralised validator ecosystem, and Binance Exchange does not own or control the network.

Over recent years, BNB Chain has developed into a sizable and active DeFi ecosystem. Users can trade on decentralised exchanges, mint NFTs, play blockchain games, and use lending and other on-chain applications. Depending on network conditions, users may also experience lower transaction costs and faster confirmations relative to some other networks.

To support additional scalability, opBNB is a Layer-2 built using Optimistic Rollup technology and the OP Stack framework. It executes transactions off the base layer and periodically batches and posts results back on-chain, helping increase throughput and reduce fees for end users.

In short, Binance supports users across both models. It operates a CeFi exchange and provides tools that connect users to on-chain ecosystems, including BNB Chain. The value of this approach becomes clearest when users can move efficiently between account-based services and on-chain activity through secure bridging mechanisms.

4 / Connecting the Dots: Bridges, Wallets, and User Connectivity

Convergence only becomes real when users can easily move value between environments without specialist knowledge. Binance’s ecosystem includes two core connectors that support this portability: 

  • Binance Bridge 2.0: One of the core pieces of infrastructure that connects the exchange with supported blockchain networks. Binance Bridge 2.0 provides a way to bridge listed and selected unlisted tokens from supported blockchains to BNB Smart Chain as BTokens, enabling use in the BNB Chain ecosystem and conversion back when needed. This can help users move assets from account-based services into on-chain applications on BNB Chain, including for assets that did not originate on BNB Chain. As with cross-chain mechanisms generally, bridges introduce additional operational, security and financial crime considerations, and appropriate safeguards should reflect the risks associated with moving assets across networks.

  • Binance Wallet: Binance Wallet is positioned as a self-custody wallet experience that uses MPC technology, removing the need for a traditional seed phrase, while still functioning as a gateway designed to facilitate user access to third-party blockchain-based applications. With this wallet, users can access multiple blockchains, trade thousands of tokens on decentralised exchanges, earn yield on DeFi platforms, and interact with dApps, all without needing to switch to external wallet software. The wallet is designed to operate on a user-directed, non-custodial basis, where users retain control of their assets and transaction approvals. Binance Wallet is designed to provide a self-custody experience through which users retain control over their assets and authorise transactions. Depending on the functionality used, the interface may facilitate access to third-party applications, aggregate liquidity or available execution routes, and support user-authorised trading features. The relevant allocation of control and responsibility should therefore be assessed by reference to the specific service and functions performed, including any transaction-routing or automated execution features.

From a regulatory perspective, these interface, routing and other access layers are increasingly assessed as potential points of intermediation*. The analysis typically turns on whether providers exercise discretion over transaction execution or routing, direct or influence user activity toward specific venues or counterparties, or otherwise perform functions analogous to financial intermediaries, as opposed to providing neutral, user-directed software tools. 

*Regulatory treatment of wallet and interface providers is fact-specific and turns on the functions performed. In the U.S., relevant broker-dealer considerations may include whether a provider takes custody, exercises discretion or control over execution or routing, brings together counterparties, or otherwise performs functions associated with intermediation. In the U.K., the ‘arranging’ perimeter distinguishes between arranging transactions and making arrangements with a view to transactions, with the analysis depending on the nature and role of the arrangements and their relationship to the relevant transaction. In both jurisdictions, the use of decentralised or non-custodial infrastructure is not, by itself, determinative. 

Where functionality is limited to neutral, user-directed technical access, the regulatory analysis should therefore focus on the functions actually performed. Relevant considerations may include whether the provider takes custody, exercises control or sufficient influence, actively facilitates regulated financial services, determines transaction routing, or otherwise performs intermediary-like functions.

To illustrate how Binance’s CeFi and DeFi offerings interplay, consider a few scenarios:

Retail path

Alice is a retail user who buys some crypto on the Binance Exchange using her debit card. After trading and accumulating BNB and USDT in her Binance account, she wants to earn higher yields. Using Binance’s Wallet feature, she transfers a portion of her BNB and USDT to her self-custody wallet. She then accesses a DeFi lending dApp on BNB Chain, and lends out her USDT to earn interest. 

The process required no complex setup, with supported bridging functionality and the wallet interface enabling Alice to move assets onto BNB Chain. Later, if Alice wants to try a new DeFi application or access an NFT marketplace, she can do so through the wallet interface. 

Alice’s journey reduces setup friction by connecting wallet access and supported cross-chain pathways through a familiar interface. At the same time, the risk and control profile changes depending on where assets are held. This may also extend to differences in product type, where users are presented with distinct disclosures and contextual information reflecting the nature and purpose of specific activities.

In a custodial CeFi account, the platform is responsible for key management and certain operational controls, while the user relies on the platform’s safeguards and processes. In self-custody, the user controls the wallet keys and transaction approvals, and assumes greater responsibility for verifying addresses, transaction details, and the risks of interacting with smart contracts and protocols.

Where assets move between a regulated service provider and a self-custody wallet, the platform may also apply risk-based transaction monitoring and other safeguards depending on the transaction, asset and applicable requirements.

If Alice later wants to convert some earnings back to fiat, she can move funds back to her Binance account and use available in-app off-ramp options to sell crypto into fiat and withdraw to a supported bank account or card, depending on her jurisdiction and available rails.

Institutional path

A large asset manager is interested in yield opportunities in crypto, but due to fiduciary duties, they require secure custody and regulatory compliance. 

The asset manager onboards to Ceffu for institutional custody and deposits assets, using custody arrangements designed for professional clients, including segregation and governance controls that support institutional risk management requirements. From there, the institution can access a range of yield and treasury-management pathways depending on its mandate and risk appetite. Some allocations may remain in account-based programs available to eligible users, while others may be deployed to on-chain strategies through structured access models and approved operational workflows.

Where intermediaries provide curated, managed, or structured access to DeFi strategies on behalf of clients, they may remain responsible for applicable regulatory and compliance obligations notwithstanding the decentralised nature of the underlying protocol, including where such access is provided through structured or discretionary workflows. This may be particularly relevant where institutions access DeFi through managed interfaces, as regulators may assess whether such access models involve intermediary functions despite the use of non-custodial or on-chain infrastructure.

This direction is increasingly reflected in international AML/CFT policy. The FATF’s 2026 DeFi report calls for financial institutions and VASPs interacting with DeFi arrangements to assess the risks of the relevant products and apply proportionate mitigation measures. The assessment may include the governance and AML/CFT controls of the DeFi arrangement, the nature of the underlying users and, where appropriate, ongoing blockchain monitoring.

For instance, an institutional custody provider can support client participation in on-chain staking on BNB Chain, or structured access to selected on-chain strategies, using defined operational workflows. The institution’s assets remain within an institutional custody framework, which can mitigate direct private key management and operational key-handling risks, while exposure is deployed to on-chain protocols where returns remain subject to smart contract, market, liquidity, and operational risks, as well as any protocol-specific governance or counterparty dependencies. 

This model may therefore provide institutions with a phased route into on-chain participation, allowing exposure to decentralised markets through controlled operational and governance frameworks rather than requiring immediate direct protocol interaction.

This illustrates how institutional access pathways may develop within Binance’s infrastructure without requiring institutions to adopt the full operational complexity of direct DeFi participation on day one.

5 / Summary of Key Components and How They Integrate

Service or Access Layer

Public Blockchain or On-chain Activity

How They Connect

Binance Exchange

BNB Chain

Bridges and wallet workflows enable moving assets for on-chain utility and back for liquidity and account-based management.

Binance Wallet

Multiple blockchain networks

Self-custody gateway designed for interacting with third-party on-chain applications.

Binance Launchpad 

On-chain token utility post-distribution

Launchpad is an IEO platform that supports project fundraising and distribution within an exchange context.

Binance Launchpool 

On-chain token exposure and distribution dynamics

Launchpool allows users to lock assets to receive token airdrops, connecting centralised participation to broader on-chain ecosystems.

Binance Custody (Ceffu) 

DeFi and exchange-linked liquidity access patterns

MirrorX is described as an off-exchange settlement that can reduce the need to move assets onto an exchange while accessing liquidity. 

6 / Strategic Value of Convergence

The strategic value of convergence is that CeDeFi can help address certain structural limitations on both sides.

CeFi can strengthen usability and onboarding, but it can also concentrate operational risk and limit portability if users cannot move freely into self-custody and on-chain markets. DeFi expands openness, choice and composability, but the user experience and risk management burden can be higher, especially for newcomers and institutions.

A CeDeFi approach aims to bring these strengths together. It supports access and safety for a broad user base while providing structured access to permissionless innovation. It also aligns with the institutional direction of travel: institutions typically begin with established venues and providers that offer robust governance, controls, and risk assessment, then broaden into on-chain activity as infrastructure, custody models, and operational standards mature. In that context, integrated ecosystems can help institutions move step-by-step, rather than relying on fragmented or untested access points.

This also aligns with emerging regulatory approaches that focus on activity and risk rather than labels such as ‘centralised’ or ‘decentralised’. In practice, this may also require clear segmentation between different categories of activity within a single platform, supported by appropriate user disclosures and risk framing, particularly where products or use cases differ materially in economic function, risk profile, or regulatory treatment.

Accordingly, the regulatory treatment of CeDeFi models is likely to depend less on whether the underlying infrastructure is described as decentralised and more on the functions performed across the value chain. Relevant considerations increasingly include practical control or sufficient influence, governance and administrative rights, active facilitation of financial services, and the nature of the relationship with users.

7 / Current Use Cases

Convergence is not theoretical. It is visible in how major financial and technology firms are using public chains for issuance, settlement, and tokenized cash-like instruments.

  • PayPal (PYUSD on Ethereum). PayPal launched an ERC-20 U.S. dollar stablecoin, redeemable 1:1 via PayPal and issued by Paxos, enabling consumers and merchants to move value on public chains while using PayPal’s familiar CeFi interfaces.

  • Visa (USDC settlement on public chains). Visa expanded stablecoin settlement to additional partners and added Solana alongside Ethereum, letting acquirers settle with Visa in USDC, an on-chain asset, through Visa’s existing CeFi network.

  • Mastercard (Multi-Token Network). Mastercard announced MTN to make digital-asset transactions secure, interoperable, and scalable for banks and fintechs, positioning card-network rails to interface with tokenized assets and public blockchains.

  • BlackRock (BUIDL tokenized fund on Ethereum). BlackRock launched its first tokenized fund with Securitize; qualified investors subscribe and receive on-chain tokens representing shares that accrue yield, a regulated investment fund using public blockchain infrastructure for tokenised ownership and related fund operations.

  • Franklin Templeton (OnChain U.S. Government Money Fund). Franklin Templeton’s registered money-market fund records ownership on public chains (Stellar; support added for Polygon), unifying regulated fund administration with on-chain registries and rails. 

  • Société Générale–FORGE (EUR CoinVertible stablecoin and digital bond). SG-FORGE issued a euro-denominated institutional stablecoin (EURCV) on Ethereum and later a digital green bond as a security token—bank-grade issuance using public-chain settlement.

  • Robinhood Wallet (self-custody with integrated swaps). Robinhood’s official wallet enables users to hold their own keys and perform Ethereum-based swaps and multi-chain transactions, giving a retail CeFi user base direct access to dApps and on-chain liquidity.

Not all of these examples constitute ‘DeFi’ in the strict sense; rather, they illustrate broader convergence between centralised financial interfaces and public blockchain-based infrastructure. However, these examples point to a consistent direction. 

Public blockchain rails are increasingly used for settlement and tokenized instruments, while familiar ‘CeFi’ interfaces and regulated entities remain central to distribution, user experience, and operating models. Taken together, they illustrate a broader convergence in which centralised financial services increasingly interact with public blockchain infrastructure, while custody, execution and control may remain allocated across different participants and layers.

This broader convergence is also giving rise to the concept of ‘TriFi’, bringing together elements of traditional finance, centralised finance and decentralised finance within increasingly connected financial ecosystems. Rather than eliminating the distinctions between these models, TriFi highlights the importance of preserving clear functional, legal and regulatory boundaries as users move between them. 

The relevant regulatory treatment should continue to follow the activity performed, the allocation of control and risk, and the role of the entities involved.

8 / Conclusion

CeFi and DeFi are converging because users and institutions prefer accessibility, flexibility and portability. This next phase of crypto adoption will be shaped by ecosystems that let users move between custodial services and self-custody experiences while maintaining appropriate safety standards, market access and usability.

Binance's vision for a unified crypto ecosystem is built around making the transition between CeFi and DeFi more accessible, secure and practical. Through its centralised exchange, Binance Wallet and supported cross-chain connectivity, alongside institutional access arrangements and independent public blockchain infrastructure such as BNB Chain, Binance provides users with pathways to trade, earn, pay and explore on-chain opportunities. 

This approach combines the scale, liquidity and familiar user experience of centralised services with greater access to decentralised innovation, while preserving the distinct custody arrangements, governance structures and responsibilities of each environment.

The barriers between CeFi and DeFi are lowering. For Binance, the most important outcome is user benefit: safer access, clearer pathways for institutions, and a more scalable route to permissionless innovation. As traditional finance increasingly connects with both models, the key question is no longer whether finance is centralised or decentralised, but how users can safely and securely engage across these different environments. 

This includes ensuring that users are able to distinguish between different categories of activity, supported by clear disclosures, appropriate segmentation, and proportionate safeguards aligned to the underlying use case.

A unified user experience does not require a unified regulatory classification 

At the user-experience level, this may increasingly be reflected in ‘superapp’ models that provide more integrated access across these different financial environments while maintaining appropriate functional and regulatory segmentation between the underlying activities. 

As regulatory approaches evolve, the treatment of hybrid CeDeFi and other hybrid models is likely to depend increasingly on the functions performed by front-end and access-layer providers, including whether they provide neutral technical access or exercise control or sufficient influence, actively facilitate financial services, or perform other intermediary-like functions. The central policy challenge will be determining where infrastructure ends and regulated financial intermediation begins based on the functions performed across the user journey.

Security

Following the 29 October security incident, Binance has continued working around the clock to trace, freeze and recover assets connected to the attack.

Binance has been granted a court order in the Abu Dhabi Global Markets (ADGM) Courts to support the recovery of assets connected to the incident. This legal action is part of our broader effort to use every lawful mechanism available to recover stolen assets and prevent funds from reaching the attackers or those who facilitate those attacks.

Why This Matters

As we have said throughout this incident, users are protected. Binance has absorbed the financial impact of the stolen funds and continues to ensure users do not bear the cost.

But protecting users is only the first step.

Our responsibility also includes pursuing the stolen assets, supporting law enforcement and industry partners, and ensuring frozen funds can be recovered through proper legal channels.

In some cases, issuers, exchanges or other partners request a formal court order before frozen assets will be released, transferred or returned. The court order Binance has obtained assists in creating that pathway.

Binance is continuing to:

  • Coordinate with issuers, exchanges, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners;

  • Trace and monitor assets connected to the attack;

  • Support the freezing and recovery of assets wherever legally possible;

This process will take time, and we will continue to provide updates as the recovery effort progresses.

Our message remains clear: Binance will not stop at reimbursing users. We will pursue the stolen assets wherever they move, using every lawful tool available.

Crypto markets failed to extend September’s 11.0% rally in October, as macroeconomic pressure and fund outflows weighed on sentiment. This blog breaks down Binance Research’s latest report, covering what shaped the month’s market performance, regulatory progress amid a stalled CLARITY Act, and the key events to watch as November unfolds.

Crypto Market Performance in October 2026

In October, total crypto market capitalization fell 9.1% to $2.70T, reversing most of September’s gains as inflation and a tech selloff weighed on markets.

September inflation rose to 3.7%, while payrolls grew just 29,000. On October 28, the Fed held rates at 3.75% to 4.00%, with two dissenters favoring a hike. Futures priced an 80–85% chance of a December increase.

The CLARITY Act remained stalled, but regulators advanced crypto rules. The OCC finalized stablecoin standards under the GENIUS Act, the CFTC opened crypto rulemaking, and the SEC’s crypto consultation closed.

BTC repeatedly fell below $80,000. Spot BTC ETFs lost $516M, while Ether ETFs saw $1.6B in outflows. Strategy bought just 851 BTC before pausing purchases, as crypto recorded its second straight October decline.

On regulation, the November 3 midterms put the focus on whether the outgoing Senate can advance CLARITY before the next Congress takes office. The window is narrow, and failure would leave the bill’s path uncertain. 

Meanwhile, the SEC’s review of comments on Regulation Crypto Assets and preparations for the GENIUS Act rules remain key developments.

The Fed held rates, but two officials dissented in favor of a hike, and the BOJ signaled a possible December move. BTC held its range for most of the month before breaking lower on October 30.

Monthly Insights is now also available in Chinese.

Macro and Policy: The Fed Holds, but Leans Higher

A softer core PCE inflation reading, the Fed’s preferred gauge, briefly eased expectations of a rate hike. The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4.00% on October 28, but the 10–2 vote leaned hawkish. Markets didn't read Chair Kevin Warsh's silence on December as dovish.

US Treasury yields stayed high, with the 30-year above 5.6% and the 10-year near 5.05%. Brent crude above $105 kept inflation risks alive. The BOJ held rates and avoided an immediate yen carry-trade unwind, but kept a December hike in play.

In equities, Alphabet fell 8–10% after hours on weak ad revenue and negative free cash flow, which raised doubts about returns on AI spending.

BTC failed to reclaim September’s $87,500 high. BTC ETF flows hovered near zero in early October before turning slightly negative. DEX volume dropped below $10 billion, roughly half its first-half level, while tokenized real-world assets rose about 10% to $8.2 billion.

The desk stays cautious through the U.S. midterms and favors low leverage and BTC over altcoins, but remains bullish over the medium term. The key test is the $75,000–$78,000 demand zone. A weekly higher low would support August’s breakout, and a move above $81,300–$83,000 would be an early positive sign. A weekly close below $75,000 would put the low $70,000s in view.

Find the Traders Worth Following With Binance Square Leaderboards

Main Takeaways

  • Binance Square is launching four Leaderboards that rank traders and streamers by their actual activity on Binance, so you can see the results behind the posts for yourself.

  • Trade Sharing ranks shared trades, Smart Money ranks futures traders, Hot Streams surfaces high-performing livestreams, and Copy Trading ranks traders you can copy.

  • The point: performance should matter more than popularity. Followers get another signal before they follow, and creators who opt in can share their results and rank.

Scroll through any social feed and it can feel like the loudest voices tend to get the most attention. If you’re deciding who to follow for trading insights, that makes it hard to tell who has the results to back up what they say. With so many creators sharing ideas, charts, and live commentary, finding the ones with a track record isn’t always easy.

Binance Square Leaderboards are built to help. Rankings are based on actual activity on Binance, so you can see the performance behind the posts and find the traders and streamers who are worth your time. This guide covers the four Square Leaderboards launching on November 12th , how each one works, and where to find them.

The Four Binance Square Leaderboards Explained

Binance Square is introducing four Leaderboards: Trade Sharing, Smart Money, Hot Streams, and Copy Trading. Because Binance connects trading and social media in one place, they draw on real trading activity. Each one is a different way to discover and follow creators on Square, so you can start with whatever interests you most.

What is the Trade Sharing Leaderboard?

The Trade Sharing Leaderboard ranks trades shared on Square by overall PnL, so you can see which shared trades are performing best across Binance, alongside the posts that explain them. When a creator shares a trade in a post using the trade widget, the Leaderboard ranks that trade by its PnL. Unlike the Smart Money Leaderboard (see below), it isn’t limited to futures.

What is the Smart Money Leaderboard?

The Smart Money Leaderboard shows which futures traders have been performing. It ranks top futures traders over a 3-day or 7-day period, using Binance Futures Smart Money, an analytics and tracking suite that helps you monitor and follow top-performing traders in real time. 

What is the Hot Streams Leaderboard?

The Hot Streams Leaderboard helps you find livestreams worth tuning into. It has two views, Trending and Live PnL. Trending ranks streams by viewership. Live PnL ranks streamers by their results while they trade live. Get straight to a stream that fits what you want to watch.

What is the Copy Trading Leaderboard?

Copy Trading lets you follow a lead trader and have their trades mirrored in your own account. This leaderboard ranks lead traders over the selected period. Each profile shows returns, follower results, assets under management, and max drawdown. You can compare lead traders side by side and weigh risk alongside performance before deciding who to follow.

How Square Leaderboards Help You Find Traders to Follow

Leaderboards put performance front and center. You can look at how traders and streamers are performing and decide who earns a spot in your busy feed. It can sometimes be hard to tell who has the results behind their posts. Leaderboards give you another signal to check.

Pick a leaderboard that matches your interest — whether that’s shared trades, futures, livestreams, or copy trading — then follow the creators who stand out. That saves you time. You can go straight to the creators who match your interests. 

When you find someone you want to keep up with, follow them from the Leaderboard to see their posts and streams. On the Copy Trading Leaderboard, you can also copy a lead trader from their profile. Remember: a ranking is a starting point. It does not represent any endorsement or recommendation to trade. Use it alongside your own research.

What Binance Square Leaderboards Mean for Creators

For creators, Binance Square Leaderboards offer visibility based on results. Think of it as a scoreboard for the work you already do on Square. If you share trades, trade futures, go live, or run a copy trading strategy, there’s a Leaderboard where your results can be seen. 

Anyone can post a market view. But a ranking can back up what you share by showing the activity behind it. It adds context to your ideas and your streams.

Your rank can travel, too. You can check it and share it, posting your position on X to bring your audience along, and invite them to follow you on Square. If you have a following elsewhere, it’s a simple way to point people to your profile. 

Leaderboards put results first, so a newcomer can be seen for what they share, whatever the size of their following.

Where to Find Binance Square Leaderboards

You can find Leaderboards in a new tab in the Binance Square menu. Open it, then switch between Trade Sharing, Smart Money, Hot Streams, and Copy Trading to explore each Leaderboard. You may also come across them through creators. When someone shares their Leaderboard rank on Binance Square or X, you can follow the link to see the full rankings. Rankings are regularly refreshed. So be sure to check back in to see who’s moving up or down.

Final Thoughts

Leaderboards bring trading and social together around a simple idea: performance should matter more than popularity. Whether you’re looking for traders to follow, streams worth watching, or a place to show your own results, there’s a Leaderboard for it. 

Trade Sharing, Smart Money, Hot Streams, and Copy Trading each offer a different way in, and creators who opt in can show the results behind their posts. Leaderboards go live on November 12th. Open Binance Square, head to the Leaderboards, and see who’s worth following.

Main Takeaways

  • Tokenized equities AUM has reached an all-time high of $4.8B, growing 164% between June and early November, according to Binance Research.

  • bStocks passed $1.5B in AUM in 145 days, making it the largest tokenized equities issuer by AUM. 

  • Adoption spans generations and regions. Gen Z makes up 46% of bStocks users, Millennials account for 78% of trading value, and emerging and frontier markets generate about 70% of volume.

The tokenized equities market sits at an all-time high of $4.8B in assets under management (AUM). Within that market, bStocks is the largest issuer by AUM, having surpassed $1.5B. The sections below look at how the market reached this point, who is using bStocks, and how users can check what backs each token.

A Brief History of Tokenized Equities

Today’s tokenized equities build on years of groundwork, from early pilots to a regulated market traded by millions of users worldwide.

2019-2021: Proof of Concept

The first wave of tokenized assets was proof-of-concept work. Franklin Templeton launched FOBXX, also known by its digital token BENJI. It was the first U.S.-registered mutual fund to record share ownership on a public blockchain. During the same period, Singapore's largest bank, DBS, settled its first S$15 million digital bond on its own regulated exchange.

2022-2024: Real-World Assets (RWA)

The second wave shifted toward yield-bearing real-world assets, led by tokenized U.S. Treasuries. Where FOBXX was a public fund open to retail investors, BlackRock brought its USD Institutional Digital Liquidity Fund (BUIDL) onto blockchain networks as a private fund for qualified institutions. This made it one of the first institutional private funds to natively integrate into DeFi.

2025-2026: Mainstream Integration

The current wave has brought mainstream integration and more legal clarity. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission issued a temporary five-year conditional exemption for tokenized securities venues, while South Korea’s official tokenized securities framework is set to take effect on February 4, 2027. 

Why Did Binance Integrate bStocks?

Our core product philosophy hasn’t changed since our founding as a digital asset exchange: we have always believed in expanding financial access worldwide. By giving users 1:1 exposure to stocks and ETFs through crypto technology, bStocks opens new pathways into traditional finance. 

Crypto-native users can diversify their exposure in a familiar format without needing a separate brokerage account, while traditional stock investors get a parallel market that stays open when Wall Street goes dark.

Who is Trading bStocks?

Data from Binance Research shows a diverse user base: roughly 56% of bStocks trading volume takes place outside regular U.S. market hours. Gen Z makes up 46% of users and trades more of its volume on weekends than any other group. Millennials hold positions the longest and account for 78% of trading value.

Users in emerging and frontier markets have generated roughly 70% of bStocks volume since launch. Many of them live in regions where U.S.-listed equities have historically been hard to access.

Are bStocks Backed 1:1?

Each token is backed 1:1 by real shares and ETFs held by a regulated custodian. Reserves are reconciled and published daily on our Proof of Collateral page, so holders can confirm their tokens are fully backed.

Final Thoughts

Tokenized equities are still a tiny fraction of traditional equities. In a market this young, our ranking  – while a welcome milestone – matters less than the direction of the entire category, which grew 81% between June and early November outside of bStocks.

We believe the way people hold and trade traditional assets may change significantly in the coming years, and we’ll continue to build and expand our bStocks offering and TradFi product suite with this, and our users, in mind.

Today’s tokenized equities build on years of groundwork, from early pilots to a regulated market traded by millions of users worldwide.

The second wave shifted toward yield-bearing real-world assets, led by tokenized U.S. Treasuries. Tokenized equities are still a tiny fraction of traditional equities. In a market this young, our ranking  – while a welcome milestone – matters less than the direction of the entire category, which grew 81% between June and early November outside of bStocks.

Understanding What Binance Is (And Isn’t) Is the Best Defense Against Scams

2026-10-20

Main Takeaways

  • Understanding the true role of Binance and practicing critical thinking are essential defenses against increasingly sophisticated scams and impersonators.

  • Binance empowers users with tools and education for financial freedom but will never provide investment advice or solicit funds.

  • In an age of advanced AI and deepfake technology, maintaining skepticism and verifying information through official channels are crucial for staying safe.

Scammers have grown unnervingly good at pretending to be us. One of the most troubling tactics we see is the deepfake: lifelike, AI-generated impersonations of Binance executives and employees soliciting money on video calls that look and sound real enough to make anyone hesitate. The personas are fabricated, but the sophistication is genuine.

Every day, people are contacted by impersonators using the names, likenesses, and even job titles of Binance staff to solicit investments or financial transactions via WhatsApp, Telegram, and other channels. It’s devastating to see people scammed out of their money, and we feel a deep responsibility to address this directly.

We always try to warn and educate our users that neither Binance nor anyone representing it will ever contact you to offer investment advice or solicit funds. But with fakes becoming so realistic, we understand the fear and confusion many feel. How can we protect ourselves in an age where the truth is so easily manipulated?

One critical defense is understanding what Binance is and isn’t, and practicing critical thinking when interacting online. This clarity can help you recognize a scam the moment it asks you to act.

Is Binance a Financial Advisor? What Binance Does and Doesn’t Do

Binance is not a financial advisor, and it will never tell you where to invest or ask you for funds. A major source of confusion is a fundamental misunderstanding of what Binance stands for. As a global financial platform, Binance has become a household name for millions, synonymous with cryptocurrency, and even broader financial opportunity. 

For some, especially those new to financial services, the perception is that Binance is a one-stop solution for all things finance: a platform, a trusted financial advisor, and even a personal guide to managing money.

But here's the truth.

Binance is committed to empowering users by building the infrastructure for the future of finance. Our mission is to increase financial freedom by providing the tools and resources to explore digital assets and traditional finance in one place. We want to make it easy for you to start your financial journey and protect your funds, while equipping you with the education to make smart, informed decisions.

However, it's important to be crystal clear: Binance is not your financial advisor. We will never tell you where to invest your money, promise guaranteed returns, or ask you for funds. Our approach is all about empowerment: we teach you how to navigate the space, make your own choices, and take control of your financial future.

This principle is at the heart of everything we do, from our leadership team down to the customer support agents who are here to help you with questions. We believe in providing the best tools and resources, but the responsibility for financial decisions lies with you.

Binance is here to support your journey, not make the choices for you. Our platform is your gateway to financial exploration, but ultimately, the power to make decisions rests with you.

How Scammers Use AI and Deepfakes to Impersonate Binance Staff

This brings us back to the danger posed by skilled impersonators. Scammers prey on people's growing interest in investing and digital finance, and the trust they have in Binance, often masquerading as Binance employees or executives to exploit the credibility we've built. With advances in AI and deepfake technology, they can create personas that look and sound real.

Technology alone isn’t what makes these scams work. Scammers succeed by exploiting confusion and misplaced trust. They count on you to believe that Binance employees might contact you with unsolicited advice or "special opportunities." This is why it's vital to remember: no one from Binance will ever tell you how to spend your money or promise you returns.

If you ever receive such a message, pause and ask yourself: Is this person empowering me with knowledge, or are they directing me to act in a specific way? Does this feel like the behavior of a helpful guide, or someone trying to exploit my trust?

When in doubt, reach out to Binance through our official support channels. We're here to help you navigate the future of finance safely, but we rely on you to exercise caution and skepticism when approached online.

How to Protect Yourself From Online Scams

One of the best ways to protect yourself is to cultivate a healthy skepticism toward anything you come across online. Just because something seems convincing doesn't mean it's trustworthy. Technology can fake appearances, but it can't replicate the integrity behind a trusted platform like Binance.

Think of Binance as your compass, not your map. We equip you with the direction and tools to explore the world of finance, but the journey is yours to own. Scammers, on the other hand, are like fake maps – promising shortcuts to success, but leading you straight into traps that result in financial loss.

As AI technology continues to evolve, distinguishing between what's real and what's fake will only get harder. That’s why it's essential to stay grounded in what you know about Binance. Know what we stand for and, just as importantly, what we don’t do. We will never promise you easy profits or solicit funds. Keep these principles in mind, and you'll be better able to spot the difference between real opportunities and dangerous scams.

At Binance, we deeply empathize with those affected by scams. We understand the gravity of losing money to bad actors and the emotional toll it takes. That’s why we're committed to educating our users and ensuring they have the tools to protect themselves.

Remember this: Binance is here to empower you, not direct you.

In an era where seeing is no longer believing, let's rely on knowledge, principles, and critical thinking to guide us. Think of it as building a firewall in your mind – one that makes you much harder to fool. Stay safe, stay informed, and remember: the power to protect yourself lies with you.

One Account, Every Market: How Binance is Building a Multi-Asset Super App

2026-06-12

This is a general educational announcement and should not be construed as solicitation to conduct any actions. Products mentioned may not be available in your jurisdiction. 

Main Takeaways

  • 7,000+ U.S. stocks and ETFs now trade alongside crypto in one Binance app and account, on a 24/5 schedule, with tokenized securities just added to the platform

  • Stock trades on Binance settle in stablecoins (USDC, USDT, USD1, $U) or BNB, reducing friction in both user experience and market access for billions of unbanked users globally. 

  • Direct stocks and ETFs, as well as the new tokenized securities functionality, mark a significant step for Binance as a financial super app, expanding from crypto trading to multi-asset trading on blockchain rails.

Every app starts as one thing. Amazon sold books before it sold everything. Grab started with rides, then grew into a payments staple across Southeast Asia.

When Binance launched in 2017, half the battle of getting into crypto was navigating the interfaces. Legacy exchanges at the time were slow, cluttered, and built for tech-savvy users. Binance focused on the basics that traders cared about: deep liquidity, faster execution, straightforward onboarding, and an accessible user experience.

Since then, we’ve continued expanding what users can access on Binance, from more trading pairs to an entire universe of products spanning payments, social, chat, and earning. Crypto remains at the center of Binance's identity. Adding stocks now establishes Binance as a complete gateway to the wider financial system. 

With Binance, you can now buy and sell over 7,000 U.S. stocks and ETFs settled in stablecoins in select jurisdictions, right alongside your crypto, in a single app.

Crypto, Stocks, and ETFs on Binance

For the last nine years, Binance has been building toward a financial system that’s more efficient, more accessible, and with fewer barriers. A core part of that vision has been creating a platform where users have greater command over their financial lives.

Over 7,000 U.S. stocks and ETFs now sit alongside crypto within one Binance app and account. Stock trading is available on an extended 24/5 schedule, because everyone should have the ability to react to market-moving news as they happen.

Alongside direct stock trading, we also launched bStocks, a tokenized securities product offering on-chain access to select U.S. stocks. With bStocks, users can trade their positions 24/7, take them off platform into their own wallets, and deploy them into DApps.

Direct stock trading and bStocks play an integral role in our super app vision, bringing crypto, equities, and on-chain finance into a unified user experience. For more details on bStocks, you can read our full announcement post. 

Removing the Friction of Multi-Asset Portfolios 

The concept of diversified investing continues to expand, spanning across multiple asset classes. Today’s investors hold crypto, equities, ETFs, and stablecoins, and they want flexibility to move between them.

On Binance, the multi-asset experience has been simplified to a few taps. Users can go from Bitcoin to widely followed U.S. equities without switching platforms.

Reducing friction also goes beyond menus and interfaces. Billions of people have a phone and an internet connection, but limited access to traditional bank infrastructure. Because stock trades settle in stablecoins on Binance, even people who previously lacked access can now trade U.S. stocks on crypto-native rails. In the first week alone, over 80% of direct stock trading volume on Binance came from emerging-market users, showing how quickly demand surfaces when friction is reduced.

Stock trading on Binance marks the first time when people from eligible jurisdictions around the world can buy and sell U.S. stocks using stablecoins in a regulated manner.

Final Thoughts

Binance started with crypto, and crypto will remain our foundation. It is still the most open, programmable, and global financial rail available today. Everything we build is guided by our core mission of advancing equitable financial access and building a more transparent and safe system for all.

Bringing stocks and ETFs into the Binance ecosystem reflects what we’ve been doing since the beginning: give users the tools they need to control their own financial futures, whether it’s through 24/5 access to stablecoin-denominated U.S. stock trading pairs or the flexibility to trade across multiple asset classes on one simple interface trusted by over 300 million users.
